subject: maths

moments.title: Newton's annus mirabilis at Woolsthorpe
moments.body:
Cambridge closes during the Great Plague. Newton (22-23) returns to his family's farm at Woolsthorpe and over 18 months works out: the method of fluxions (calculus), the spectrum of white light, the inverse-square law of gravitation, and the binomial theorem.

It is one of the most productive periods in the history of science. He shares almost none of it publicly.
moments.takeaway: A young man invents calculus during plague isolation — and tells almost no one for two decades.

moments.title: Leibniz publishes calculus
moments.who: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, Hanover and Paris
moments.body:
Leibniz, having worked out calculus independently over the years 1675-1684, publishes his version in Acta Eruditorum: differential calculus (1684) and integral calculus (1686). His notation — dx, dy, the elongated integral sign — is clean, suggestive, and easily extensible.

Mainland European mathematicians adopt Leibniz's calculus rapidly. Newton's fluxion notation is awkward and never spreads.
moments.takeaway: Leibniz publishes first and uses better notation. Continental Europe learns calculus from him.

moments.title: Newton publishes Principia
moments.body:
Newton finally publishes 'Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica' — the foundations of classical mechanics. He derives Kepler's laws of planetary motion from his three laws of motion and the inverse-square law of gravitation.

The Principia is mathematically dense and uses geometric proofs (rather than calculus, which Newton had not yet publicly developed). It is one of the most important scientific books ever written.
moments.takeaway: Newton's physics arrives. Hidden inside are calculus-based derivations he chooses to present geometrically.

moments.title: The priority dispute
moments.body:
Nicolas Fatio de Duillier, a Swiss mathematician and Newton ally, publicly accuses Leibniz of plagiarism in 1699. Tensions escalate.

The Royal Society appoints a committee to adjudicate in 1711. The committee is hand-picked by Newton. The final report (largely written anonymously by Newton himself) finds for Newton in 1712. Leibniz dies in 1716 with his reputation in tatters in Britain.

Mainland Europe continues to credit Leibniz. Britain, loyal to Newton, retains fluxion notation and falls behind continental mathematics by a century.
moments.takeaway: Both invented calculus independently. The British scientific establishment poisons international mathematics for generations.

moments.title: Cauchy and Weierstrass — rigorous foundations
moments.body:
Both Newton's 'evanescent quantities' and Leibniz's 'infinitesimals' had philosophical problems. George Berkeley's 1734 attack 'The Analyst' called them 'ghosts of departed quantities'.

Cauchy (Cours d'Analyse, 1821) and later Weierstrass replace infinitesimals with rigorous limit definitions using epsilon and delta. Calculus becomes mathematically respectable.
moments.takeaway: Rigorous foundations come 150 years after the original invention. The intuition came first; the rigour followed.

now.title: Calculus today
now.body:
Calculus is the language of modern physics, engineering, economics, and most of applied mathematics. Leibniz's notation is universal. Computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Maple, SymPy) do most undergraduate calculus automatically.

Generalisations: calculus of variations (Lagrangian mechanics), distribution theory (Schwartz, for functions like Dirac delta), non-standard analysis (Robinson, rigorous infinitesimals), stochastic calculus (Itô, for random processes), discrete calculus.
now.open_questions: Can we automate higher-level calculus reasoning? Are there number systems that simplify the infinitesimal approach? Can calculus be made more accessible to learners struggling with the conceptual leap from algebra?

reflection: Newton was famously cruel to rivals. He used his power at the Royal Mint to destroy counterfeiters and his power at the Royal Society to destroy Leibniz's reputation. Leibniz was a diplomat, philosopher and polymath spread across many projects. Both invented one of the most important mathematical tools in history independently. How do we evaluate scientific contributions when personal character and institutional power so deeply shape who gets remembered?
